Nature Club / MAKE · LEARN · DISCOVER

Make a sound map.

Slow down. There is a world to hear.

Ages 3–1215 minOutdoors or by a window

A sound map records what you hear instead of what you see. A garden, schoolyard or open window can all be listening places. Stay in one spot and notice quiet sounds as well as loud ones.

Let's get started ↓Get the activity sheet
BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Gather your bits.

Tick things off as you get ready.

A note for grown-ups

Stay with an adult away from roads, water edges and unfamiliar animals. Keep your eyes open if that helps you stay aware of your surroundings. Do not follow a sound into an unsafe area. Listen from indoors if outdoors is unsuitable.

A little more guidance ↗
ONE STEP AT A TIME

Let's make it happen.

  1. Choose your listening spot

    Sit or stand comfortably in a safe place. Draw a small X in the centre of your paper to show where you are.

  2. Listen for a short while

    Pause for about one minute. You may hear birds, wind, voices or traffic. There is no need for complete silence.

  3. Mark the directions

    For each sound, draw a simple symbol on the side of the X where you heard it. A wavy line might mean wind; a dot might mean a tapping sound.

  4. Listen again

    Spend another minute listening. Add new sounds and circle any that repeat. Place distant sounds farther from the X if you can judge their distance.

  5. Compare your discoveries

    Share your map. Explain your symbols and describe one sound that was easy to miss. Return another time and see what changes.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

What's happening here?

Listening from a fixed position helps connect sounds with direction and distance. A symbol lets you record a sound without needing to spell its name. Different listeners may notice different things.

Keep the wondering going.

  • Which sound was closest? Which seemed far away?
  • What changed between your two listening moments?
  • Which sounds might be different in the evening?

Make it work for you.

Keep it simple

Listen for just 20–30 seconds. Point toward a sound and let an adult draw the mark.

Take it further

Create a key for natural and human-made sounds. Compare maps made at the same place at two different times.

Not quite going to plan?

Too much background noise? Try a quieter place with an adult or listen by a window. If hearing is limited, adapt this to a movement map and mark leaves, shadows or other visible changes.
